results.description:
China has bought about €290bn of Russian fossil fuels since the EU bans.

India about €170bn. Türkiye about €110bn.

The EU itself still bought about €80bn, mostly gas plus pipeline crude.

China and India took 87% of Russia’s crude.

September still brought Moscow €625m a day.

Washington has just waived its new sanctions on buyers too.

The barrels changed customers. 

Moscow still gets paid.

results.description:
Senators Urge Trump to Reverse Diesel Deal With Putin https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/us/politics/trump-putin-russia-diesel-senate.html?smid=tw-share 

Lindsey Graham Act of 2026: Trump Defangs His Own Law

(Enthusiasm to kill Russian economy by blocking its oil sale proved futile. The infamous Lindsey Graham Act of 100% tariff on China & India for buying Russian oil has been suspended. With this change America will import Russian diesel and may spell end of Ukraine war.)

Barely a month after the Lindsey Graham Act of 2026 gained bipartisan support in Congress, President Donald Trump has effectively defanged it. The law threatened 100% tariffs on goods imported from countries such as India and China if they continued buying Russian oil. Trump’s executive order has now put those tariff provisions on hold.
If this holds, it is welcome news for the global economy.

The law remains on the books, and repealing it could be difficult. But implementation rests with the Trump administration, which has chosen not to enforce its most damaging provisions—for now. Trump signed the legislation after both chambers of Congress approved it, only to retreat from its central objective now.
Washington is becoming a theatre of political contradictions. Lindsey Graham spent two years pushing for tougher measures against Russia, arguing that cutting Moscow’s oil revenue was essential to ending the Ukraine war. Yet his proposed 100% tariffs on India and China risked disrupting global trade, raising consumer prices and wrecking decades of economic integration. China would have borne the greatest impact, potentially derailing efforts to stabilize U.S.–China trade. India, too, would have suffered unnecessarily.

Graham may now be regretting his unwavering support for Trump’s MAGA agenda. His sanctions strategy ignored a basic economic reality: punishing major oil buyers does not automatically end a war. It can instead destabilize markets and hurt the countries imposing the punishment.

The oil crisis has made that reality impossible to ignore. With the Strait of Hormuz closed and millions of barrels of Russian oil potentially threatened, the world cannot afford another major disruption to supply. American gasoline prices have reportedly surged, while diesel shortages have become serious enough for Washington to consider importing Russian diesel.

The contradiction is striking. Trump has reportedly urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop attacking Russian refineries, which supply much of Russia’s diesel. Zelensky’s continued strikes risk further escalation with Moscow, even as fuel shortages threaten the U.S. economy.

The political consequences could be severe. Rising gasoline and diesel prices threaten Republican prospects in the midterm elections, turning foreign policy into a domestic liability. Economic reality, electoral calculations and the danger of a trade war have apparently outweighed Graham’s punitive ambitions.

Russia, China, India and the wider global economy can breathe a little easier. Supporters of Graham’s legislation may protest Trump’s willingness to resume Russian fuel imports, but the administration faces a choice between ideological posturing and practical necessity.
Trump has chosen necessity—for now. The episode exposes the weakness of a policy that threatens sweeping economic punishment without adequately considering its consequences. 

Sanctions may be politically attractive, but when they endanger energy supplies, trade and voters’ wallets, even their strongest advocates may have to retreat.

results.title: Per CREA for September 2026, the EU bought EUR 1.7 bn in Russian fossil fuels (third-largest after China and India), mainly pipeline gas (EU
results.description:
Per CREA for September 2026, the EU bought EUR 1.7 bn in Russian fossil fuels (third-largest after China and India), mainly pipeline gas (EUR 817 mn) and LNG (EUR 615 mn), plus EUR 290 mn crude via Druzhba. 

Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply over 300k tons of diesel immediately, plus 500k in November, 1 mn thereafter, and potentially 3 mn more (up to ~4.8 mn tons total), with a temporary sanctions waiver until April 2027.
